{{for|the theorem about simplexes|Sperner's lemma}}
{{short description|Theorem on the largest antichain of sets}}
'''Sperner's theorem''', in [[discrete mathematics]], describes the largest possible [[family of sets|families]] of [[finite set]]s none of which contain any other sets in the family. It is one of the central results in [[Extremal combinatorics|extremal set theory]].  It is named after [[Emanuel Sperner]], who published it in 1928.

This result is sometimes called Sperner's lemma, but the name "[[Sperner's lemma]]" also refers to an unrelated result on coloring triangulations.  To differentiate the two results, the result on the size of a Sperner family is now more commonly known as Sperner's theorem.

==Statement==
A [[family of sets]] in which none of the sets is a strict subset of another is called a [[Sperner family]], or an [[antichain]] of sets, or a clutter. For example, the family of <math>k</math>-element subsets of an <math>n</math>-element set is a Sperner family. No set in this family can contain any of the others, because a containing set has to be strictly bigger than the set it contains, and in this family all sets have equal size. The value of <math>n</math> that makes this example have as many sets as possible is <math>n/2</math> if <math>n</math> is even, or either of the nearest integers to <math>n/2</math> if <math>n</math> is odd. For this choice, the number of sets in the family is <math>\tbinom{n}{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}</math>.

Sperner's theorem states that these examples  are the largest possible Sperner families over an <math>n</math>-element set.
Formally, the theorem states that, 
#for every Sperner family <math>S</math> whose union has a total of <math>n</math> elements, <math>|S| \le \tbinom{n}{\lfloor n/2\rfloor},</math> and
#equality holds if and only if <math>S</math> consists of all subsets of an <math>n</math>-element set that have size <math>\lfloor n/2\rfloor</math> or all that have size <math>\lceil n/2\rceil</math>.

==Partial orders==
Sperner's theorem can also be stated in terms of [[partial order width]]. The family of all subsets of an <math>n</math>-element set (its [[power set]]) can be [[partially ordered]] by set inclusion; in this partial order, two distinct elements are said to be incomparable when neither of them contains the other. The width of a partial order is the largest number of elements in an [[antichain]], a set of pairwise incomparable elements. Translating this terminology into the language of sets, an antichain is just a Sperner family, and the width of the partial order is the maximum number of sets in a Sperner family.
Thus, another way of stating Sperner's theorem is that the width of the [[inclusion order]] on a power set is <math>\tbinom{n}{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}</math>.

A [[Graded poset|graded]] [[partially ordered set]] is said to have the [[Sperner property of a partially ordered set|Sperner property]] when one of its largest antichains is formed by a set of elements that all have the same rank. In this terminology, Sperner's theorem states that the partially ordered set of all subsets of a finite set, partially ordered by set inclusion, has the Sperner property.

== Proof ==
There are many proofs of Sperner's theorem, each leading to different generalizations (see {{harvtxt|Anderson|1987}}).

The following proof is due to {{harvtxt|Lubell|1966}}. Let <math>s_k</math> denote the number of <math>k</math>-sets in <math>S</math>. For all <math>0\le k\le n</math>,

<math display=block>{n \choose \lfloor{n/2}\rfloor} \ge {n \choose k}</math>

and, thus,

<math display=block>{s_k \over {n \choose \lfloor{n/2}\rfloor}} \le {s_k \over {n \choose k}}.</math>

Since <math>S</math> is an antichain, one can sum over the above inequality from <math>k=0</math> to <math>n</math> and then apply the [[Lubell–Yamamoto–Meshalkin inequality]] to obtain

<math display=block>\sum_{k=0}^n{s_k \over {n \choose \lfloor{n/2}\rfloor}} \le \sum_{k=0}^n{s_k \over {n \choose k}} \le 1,</math>

and multiplying both sides by the binomial coefficient in the denominator of the left hand side gives

<math display=block> |S| = \sum_{k=0}^n s_k \le {n \choose \lfloor{n/2}\rfloor}.</math>

This completes the proof of part 1.

To have equality, all the inequalities in the preceding proof must be equalities.  Since 
<math display=block>{n \choose \lfloor{n/2}\rfloor} = {n \choose k}</math>
if and only if <math>k = \lfloor{n/2}\rfloor</math> or <math>\lceil{n/2}\rceil,</math> equality implies that <math>S</math> consists only of sets of sizes <math>\lfloor{n/2}\rfloor</math> or <math>\lceil{n/2}\rceil.</math>  For even <math>n</math> that concludes the proof of part 2.

For odd <math>n</math> there are additional complications, omitted here. See {{harvtxt|Anderson|1987}}, pp.&nbsp;3–4.

==Generalizations==
There are several generalizations of Sperner's theorem for subsets of <math>\mathcal P(E),</math> the poset of all subsets of <math>E</math>.

===No long chains===
A ''chain'' is a subfamily <math>\{S_0,S_1,\dots,S_r\} \subseteq \mathcal P(E)</math> that is totally ordered, i.e., <math>S_0 \subset S_1\subset \dots\subset S_r</math> (possibly after renumbering).  The chain has <math>r+1</math> members and '''length''' <math>r</math>.  An ''<math>r</math>-chain-free family'' (also called an ''<math>r</math>-family'') is a family of subsets of <math>E</math> that contains no chain of length <math>r</math>.  {{harvtxt|Erdős|1945}} proved that the largest size of an <math>r</math>-chain-free family is the sum of the <math>r</math> largest binomial coefficients <math>\tbinom{n}{i}</math>.  The case <math>r=1</math> is Sperner's theorem.

==={{mvar|p}}-compositions of a set===
In the set <math>\mathcal P(E)^p</math> of <math>p</math>-tuples of subsets of <math>E</math>, one <math>p</math>-tuple <math>(S_1,\dots,S_p)</math> is less than or equal to (≤) another one, <math>(T_1,\dots,T_p),</math> if <math>S_i \subseteq T_i</math> for each <math>i=1,2,\dots,p</math>. <math>(S_1,\dots,S_p)</math> is a ''<math>p</math>-composition'' of <math>E</math> if the sets <math>S_1,\dots,S_p</math> form a partition of <math>E</math>.  {{harvtxt|Meshalkin|1963}} proved that the maximum size of an antichain of <math>p</math>-compositions is the largest <math>p</math>-multinomial coefficient <math>\tbinom{n}{n_1\ n_2\ \dots\ n_p},</math> that is, the coefficient in which all <math>n_i</math> are as nearly equal as possible (i.e., they differ by at most 1).  Meshalkin proved this by proving a generalized LYM inequality.

The case <math>p=2</math> is Sperner's theorem, because then <math>S_2 = E \setminus S_1</math> and the assumptions reduce to the sets <math>S_1</math> being a Sperner family.

===No long chains in {{mvar|p}}-compositions of a set===
{{harvtxt|Beck|Zaslavsky|2002}} combined the Erdös and Meshalkin theorems by adapting Meshalkin's proof of his generalized LYM inequality.  They showed that the largest size of a family of <math>p</math>-compositions such that the sets in the <math>i</math>th position of the <math>p</math>-tuples, ignoring duplications, are <math>r</math>-chain-free, for every <math>i = 1,2,\dots,p-1</math> (but not necessarily for <math>i=p</math>), is not greater than the sum of the <math>r^{p-1}</math> largest <math>p</math>-multinomial coefficients.

===Projective geometry analog===
In the [[finite projective space]] <math>\operatorname{PG}(d,q)</math>
of dimension <math>d</math> over a [[finite field]] of order <math>q</math>, let <math>\mathcal L(p,F_q)</math> be the family of all subspaces.  When partially ordered by set inclusion, this family is a lattice.  {{harvtxt|Rota|Harper|1971}} proved that the largest size of an antichain in <math>\mathcal L(p,F_q)</math> is the largest [[Gaussian coefficient]]
<math display=block>\begin{bmatrix} d+1 \\ k\end{bmatrix};</math>
this is the projective-geometry analog, or ''<math>q</math>-analog'', of Sperner's theorem.

They further proved that the largest size of an <math>r</math>-chain-free family in <math>\mathcal L(p,F_q)</math> is the sum of the <math>r</math> largest Gaussian coefficients.  Their proof is by a projective analog of the LYM inequality.

===No long chains in {{mvar|p}}-compositions of a projective space===
{{harvtxt|Beck|Zaslavsky|2003}} obtained a Meshalkin-like generalization of the Rota&ndash;Harper theorem.  In <math>\operatorname{PG}(d,q)</math>, a '''Meshalkin sequence''' of length <math>p</math> is a sequence <math>(A_1,\ldots,A_p)</math> of projective subspaces such that no proper subspace of <math>\operatorname{PG}(d,q)</math> contains them all and their dimensions sum to <math>d-p+1</math>.  The theorem is that a family of Meshalkin sequences of length <math>p</math> in <math>\operatorname{PG}(d,q)</math>, such that the subspaces appearing in position <math>i</math> of the sequences contain no chain of length <math>r</math> for each <math>i = 1,2,\dots,p-1,</math> is not more than the sum of the largest <math>r^{p-1}</math> of the quantities 
<math display=block>\begin{bmatrix} d+1 \\ n_1\ n_2\ \dots\ n_p \end{bmatrix} q^{s_2(n_1,\ldots,n_p)},</math> 
where
<math display=block>\begin{bmatrix} d+1 \\ n_1\ n_2\ \dots\ n_p \end{bmatrix}</math>
(in which we assume that <math>d+1 = n_1+\cdots+n_p</math>) denotes the <math>p</math>-Gaussian coefficient 
<math display=block>\begin{bmatrix} d+1 \\ n_1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} d+1-n_1 \\ n_2 \end{bmatrix} \cdots \begin{bmatrix} d+1-(n_1+\cdots+n_{p-1} )\\ n_p \end{bmatrix}</math> 
and 
<math display=block>s_2(n_1,\ldots,n_p) := n_1n_2 + n_1n_3 + n_2n_3 + n_1n_4 + \cdots + n_{p-1}n_p,</math> 
the second [[elementary symmetric function]] of the numbers <math>n_1, n_2, \dots, n_p.</math>
